Employment: Retired (35+ yrs high-school teacher); works ~40 hrs/wk as a volunteer facilitator
Education: Master's (1st year completed; stopped due to vision)
Vision: Totally blind; regained some color perception after eye surgery ~2 yrs ago. Vision loss from retinopathy of prematurity (incubator oxygen); progressive, total loss by 2000.
Mobility: Tapping cane outdoors; uses a broom indoors as a cane substitute
Usage: As often as possible; some days daily, limited by reliability
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Be My Eyes, Seeing AI, Aira, screen reader / VoiceOver, ChatGPT (daily), iPhone, 2nd phone (workaround)
Notable: Author of the first instructional cookbook for blind/VI people (toaster-bag method); facilitates a group of ~77 people learning the glasses; local TV/YouTube presence. High tech fluency at 79.
Super-user / community facilitator (P001: High tech fluency; teaches dozens of others; tolerates friction and improvises workarounds (cold-start ritual, second phone). Provides ecosystem-level insight.Needs: Advanced concurrency (glasses + phone), reliability, real support, longer battery.
Independent daily generalist (P002): Younger; daily hands-free use across cooking, parenting, church, deliveries, self-care, and learning. Values discreetness and continuity.Needs: Person recognition/locating, discreet interaction, session continuity, dependable everyday accuracy.
Hobby specialist, desk-bound (P003): Deep, repeated use in one domain. Long multi-turn research sessions. Mobility limits and a live-in aide keep everything else off the device.Needs: Training on what it can do, accuracy on niche facts, concurrent phone use, source citation.
Outdoor-first bilingual professional (P0: Wears them from the front door onward. Grocery, restaurants, museums, buses. Strong AI fluency from professional use, and a strict data-hygiene rule.Needs: Prescription that supports near and far, first-language support, scoped answers, open messaging and apps, longer battery.
Recent-onset under-user (P010): Bought with more sight than she has now. Knows the features exist, does not reach for them. Fit, battery anxiety, AI shyness and available family all compete with the device.Needs: Frames that fit, longer battery, prompts and training, safe failure recovery.
Enthusiast tester, non-Meta device (P011: Buys into a blind-market device with blind designers, files bug reports, tests in cars, airports and racetracks. Rates it 4.5 to 5 while listing a dozen changes.Needs: Lower latency, offline reading, wearer voice recognition, frame sizes, vendor continuity.
Content creator, camera-first (P005): Bought the glasses to shoot point of view video, not to read. Head is the tripod. Everything downstream, framing, record state, file names, audio bleed, bystander privacy, is unsupported.Needs: framing coaching, unmistakable record state, usable clip names, capture-time privacy flags, lower lag.
Working consultant, patience-limited (P0: Wants daily use, gets intermittent use. Job tasks with an employer's clock on them. Product packaging designed to defeat OCR. Falls back to paid interpreters rather than volunteers.Needs: fewer retries, honest failure reasons, integration that sets itself up, contrast handling.
Accessibility professional, sceptical po: Maximum technical fluency, minimum trust. Retires a use case on one fabrication. Uses the device mostly as open-ear headphones with a pocket braille controller.Needs: no fabrication, hedging when unsure, text handed off to the phone, audible output in noise, no ad targeting.
Low-vision professional, document-first: Substantial residual sight, so he verifies what he is told. Board papers, agendas and letters are the whole use case. Runs a full smart home and buys appliances by contrast.Needs: face enrollment and locating, better camera in low light, audible output on the street, location grounding, two-device pairing.
Low-vision academic, reading-first (P014: Forty-eight years of progressive loss, so every workaround predates the device. Reads letters, placards, museum text and department papers. Measures the glasses against a desktop magnifier and a legacy universal reader, not against other glasses.Needs: walking directions spoken turn by turn, a way to send a capture without the phone, region-level questions on a page, a tool voice rather than a companion voice.
Practical daily reader, low exploration: Daily use, narrow repertoire, almost no feature discovery. Never tried Live AI. Learns about the product from owner groups rather than the vendor. Prompts precisely because he taught himself to after bad reads.Needs: awareness prompts, framing coaching, longer runtime, a free continuous mode.
Blind creator and tester, AI-sceptical (: Highest technical fluency in the new group and the lowest opinion of the on-board AI. Routes visual work to human volunteers through the camera and uses the glasses mostly as a microphone and a headset. Frames hallucination as a property of AI rather than a defect of this product.Needs: a camera that a remote helper can use, honest declining, faster connect, a replaceable battery, less pressure on the face.
Social navigator, continuous narration (: Uses the glasses to move through venues, find exits, meet people and identify clothing. Runs a third-party always-on narration app alongside and has the sharpest requirements for it: filter, pause, priority, speed.Needs: a content filter, a pause gesture, head-level hazard calls, spoken framing guidance, directional answers rather than yes or no.
Audio-first under-user, unaware of the A: Wears them daily for podcasts and mail. Reads ingredient labels for the first time in her life. Has never held a conversation with the assistant, never asked a follow-up question, and did not know the device ran a general AI until the interview said so.
Cane-verified daily user, safety-motivat: Came to wearable cameras looking for evidence against strangers who approach her, and found the AI afterwards. Uses the cane to check every spatial claim the glasses make. Rejects continuous mode over its voice quality.
Progressive low-vision professional, dis: Uses it to pull one fact out of a dense document at work. Substantial residual reading vision, so the glasses save time rather than provide access. Wants an overlay drawn on the world rather than more speech.

Household: 1 other person; has dependent(s), a young son
Vision: No vision (totally blind); 6 years at this level. Has light sensitivity.
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Be My Eyes, Seeing AI (currency), Aira, AuraCam / Envision-style glasses reference, Meta app, cane
Notable: Uses glasses across cooking, parenting, church, deliveries, self-care/hair, language learning. Values discreetness and hands-free operation. Cared for a child during the interview.
Super-user / community facilitator (P001: Blocked by the phone and glasses conflict and stranded by e-commerce support; a high-value evangelist if unblocked.
Independent daily generalist (P002): Adopts smoothly via app onboarding; growth limited by missing person-recognition and social-setting friction.
Hobby specialist, desk-bound (P003): Already satisfied within a narrow lane. Growth depends entirely on activation support, not features.
Outdoor-first bilingual professional (P0: Highest daily reliance in the set. Ceiling is set by lens optics and a closed app platform, not by the AI.
Recent-onset under-user (P010): The highest-upside segment. Nothing is broken. The gap is activation.
Enthusiast tester, non-Meta device (P011: Ceiling is vendor scale and survival, not user willingness. The clearest source of comparative design lessons.
Content creator, camera-first (P005): Lowest satisfaction in the study and still using them daily for one task. An entire persona the product does not know exists.
Working consultant, patience-limited (P0: Blocked by time per read rather than by any missing feature. The clearest case for measuring retries instead of capability.
Accessibility professional, sceptical po: The hardest user to win and the most valuable to win. Her stated route back is other users reporting improvement, not vendor claims.
Low-vision professional, document-first: Highest satisfaction and trust in the new group, both earned through independent verification. Also the clearest evidence that partial sight is a distinct design target.
Low-vision academic, reading-first (P014: High satisfaction inside a narrow reading lane. His ceiling is set by the world's touchscreens and by the phone conflict, not by description quality.
Practical daily reader, low exploration: Nothing is broken and nothing is growing. The clearest activation case in the set: a competent daily user who does not know what he owns.
Blind creator and tester, AI-sceptical (: Rates the AI 2 of 5 and still wears them. The value he keeps is the human on the other end of the camera.
Social navigator, continuous narration (: The first participant to have lived with continuous description rather than wished for it. His complaints are the specification for the feature everyone else is asking for.
Audio-first under-user, unaware of the A: The clearest activation case in the study. Nothing is broken. The mental model is the ceiling.
Cane-verified daily user, safety-motivat: High use, high trust, and a verification habit built from a mobility aid rather than from the device.
Progressive low-vision professional, dis: Adoption is running ahead of need and will meet it. Names auditory processing as the barrier to screen readers.

Device: Ray-Ban Meta (gen 2, received day before interview)
Mobility: Wheelchair pushed by aide after a fall and shoulder replacement; walks with difficulty
Device tenure: ~2 years; gen 2 received the day before the interview
Usage: ~5 sessions a week, about an hour each, at his desk
Tools they use: Meta glasses, ChatGPT handoff, Be My Eyes (historic), Discogs and Google via the AI, live-in aide
Notable: Collects 45 RPM vinyl. Uses the glasses almost entirely for record labels, chart history and valuation lookups. The phone-and-glasses conflict broke the interview demo live. Wants training on what the device can do.

Employment: Part-time contractor, accountant, Puerto Rico company
Household: Lives alone, no dependents, no pets
Vision: Juvenile glaucoma, diagnosed at 18. 100% blind right eye, 85% blind left, ~15% residual vision. Sight lost over 6 months, 2022 to 2023.
Usage: Every day, worn from the moment she leaves the house
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Seeing AI (AI mode and volunteers), translation app, Messenger, ChatGPT and Gemini at work, Siri, second pair of reading glasses
Notable: Only participant with prescription lenses and the only non-native English speaker. Names personal security, not convenience, as the reason to go hands-free. Runs a strict data-hygiene rule at work.

Device: Ray-Ban Meta (Black Friday purchase, generation not stated)
Employment: Social Security disability; self-described self-employed, building social media channels, no income from them
Education: Bachelor of Science, plus online courses and a non-secular doctorate in metaphysics
Vision: Retinitis pigmentosa. Light perception only in the right eye, 4 over 200 in the left. Diagnosed 2005, legally blind 2010, progressive.
Device tenure: About 5.5 months (Black Friday deal, late November)
Usage: Two to three times a week, mostly for capture
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Be My Eyes volunteers, ChatGPT (daily, also for troubleshooting and captions), VoiceOver, Final Cut Pro, Audible, guide dog and cane. Learning braille.
Notable: Only content creator in the study. Bought the glasses to shoot point of view video for four social platforms under the handle blind outdoorsman. Lowest overall satisfaction in the set at about 2. Uses one chatbot to troubleshoot the other. Wants bystander data flagged automatically in his own footage. Offered his channels to the research team.

Employment: Mary Kay beauty consultant; actively seeking other employment; under $40,000
Household: 1 other person; one dog; no dependents
Vision: No vision at all. Totally blind since birth.
Mobility: White cane; has used a guide dog previously
Usage: Intermittent, well below intended. Would like daily.
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Aira, Seeing AI, Be My Eyes AI, ChatGPT (building an app), JAWS, Alexa with a smart microwave, cane.
Notable: Only participant to demonstrate the device live during the interview, including a failed read and a successful retry after being coached by the interviewer on where to hold the bottle. Names patience as the limiting resource six times. States flatly that the glasses must never be used as a mobility tool. Building a makeup confidence app for blind women.

Device: Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, no display, generation uncertain
Employment: Part-time, accessibility and research, disability studies; under $25,000
Household: 2 family members; a dog, not a service dog; no dependents
Vision: Congenitally blind, no light perception. Since birth.
Usage: Once or twice a week. Mostly audio, calls and time, little image description.
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Aira, Seeing AI, ChatGPT, Hable controller, Microsoft Soundscape, Apple Watch, cane.
Notable: Works professionally in accessibility research and cites published reports. Used the first-generation Aira wireless glasses in 2017. Retires a use case after a single fabrication. Uses research interviewing technique to avoid leading the AI. The only participant whose privacy objection is ad targeting, and it is conditional on accuracy.

Employment: Retired professor; board member of several NGOs and companies; healthcare AI advisor
Vision: Retinitis pigmentosa. About 50 percent vision, legally blind under Illinois law. About 15 years at this level. Cannot recognise faces beyond 2 to 3 feet. Sight weakens through the day.
Mobility: Regular cane for balance, not a white cane
Device tenure: Not stated; gen 2, in regular use
Usage: Daily and out of the house. Six hours of wear reported the day before the interview.
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Alexa, Google AI, BARD audiobooks, VoiceOver, prescription magnifier, app-controlled blinds, washer and dishwasher, tactile bump dots.
Notable: Only participant with substantial residual vision and the only one who can verify a reading independently, using a prescription magnifier. Helped build a hospital sepsis alert AI and has caught radiology AI errors. Buys banks and appliances by readability. Wants face enrollment from his contact photos to find a friend in a ballroom.

Persona: Late-blind vocal coach, audio-first, unaware of the AI
Device: Ray-Ban Meta, generation not stated (2 to 3 hour runtime suggests gen 1)
Employment: Part-time vocal coach, teaches singing online; laid off from a Microsoft-acquired company
Education: Two bachelor's degrees (contemporary vocal, music business)
Household: Lives alone; no dependents; no pets (allergic)
Location: North Carolina (moved from New York; trained at Blind Inc, Minneapolis)
Vision: Lost sight at age 9. Retina scarred, no central vision, some peripheral. 3000/20 left, 1000/20 right. Sees light, dark and some colour.
Mobility: Long white cane, no guide dog. Did not start using a cane until her 30s.
Device tenure: About 8 to 9 months (gifted last fall by a nurse from her church)
Usage: Daily, mostly as an audio headset. Task use is occasional and confined to a familiar store and her parents’ home.
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Be My Eyes (volunteer), Seeing AI, ChatGPT (daily), VoiceOver on Mac, One Touch Reader, braille dots and rubber-band labelling
Notable: Did not know the glasses ran a general AI. Describes them as a one-step reader. Reads ingredient labels for the first time and changed what she buys. Reports the device disconnecting when she looks down.

Household: 2 others (husband, daughter); 3 cats and a dog
Vision: Optic nerve. No colour vision, dark and shadowy, some central vision. Left eye 2020, right eye lost just over a year ago.
Usage: Irregular; sometimes weeks or a month between uses
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Be My Eyes, Seeing AI, VoiceOver, prism reading glasses, family members
Notable: Recent vision loss, bought with more sight than she has now. The clearest under-use case in the set. Fell off a treadmill troubleshooting a dropped audio connection. Interview itself shifted her intent to use it more.

Persona: Enthusiast tester on a different device
Device: EchoVision by AGIGA (blind-market device, not Meta)
Vision: Light, colour, shadow, shape and movement, likely under 2%. Since birth.
Usage: Irregular; heavy in bursts, tested on a road trip
Tools they use: EchoVision, Be My Eyes, Aira, Seeing AI (on phone), ChatGPT, Gemini, Alexa, cane
Notable: Only non-Meta device in the study. Beta-tester relationship with a small vendor that employs blind designers. Live AI in a moving car, at an airport and at a racetrack. Plans a NASCAR race in September as the real test.

Persona: Daily practical user, cane-verified, camera-first arrival
Employment: Not in paid work; survivor benefits; volunteer ministry, moving into blind ministry
Education: High school, plus a semester or two of college
Household: 1 other person; one cat (Stormy); no dependents
Vision: Retinitis pigmentosa from birth. Now near-total: a constant bright white field with occasional shadow. About 4 to 5 years at this level.
Usage: Every day, from leaving the flat onwards. Obstacles, colours, labels, aisles, product research.
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Tap2C (colour), Seeing AI, RunGo, Soundscape, VoiceOver, spare batteries
Notable: Came looking for a wearable camera for personal safety rather than an AI. Uses the cane to verify what the glasses report. Ran a live product query on camera during the interview. Rejects continuous mode over its voice.

Persona: Late-onset low-vision teacher, document-first, early adopter
Device: Ray-Ban Meta, non-prescription blue blocker with polycarbonate lenses
Gender: Stated "Mail" at L479 (transcription unclear). Interviewer uses "she" at L193; participant refers to "my husband" at L291. Verify before reporting.
Household: 1 other person; two dogs (a standard Golden Doodle, a toy poodle); no dependents
Location: New Jersey, close to New York City
Vision: Neuropathy of the optic nerve, about 5 years. Multiple blind spots, poor peripheral vision and poor depth perception. Right eye worse than left. Progressive. Beginning to lose red and orange discrimination.
Mobility: Owns a cane, rarely uses it. No guide dog.
Usage: Daily. Worn almost constantly, though features are used far less often than the device is worn.
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Be My Eyes (phone only, never with the glasses), ChatGPT, Maps app through the glasses speakers, Oko (tried once), a magnifier
Notable: Also has ADHD and uses the timers for it. Stopped by a Broadway usher who assumed he was recording. Reports a false negative on an expiration date. Wants an in-lens visual overlay rather than more speech.

Device: Ray-Ban Meta (bought on sale July 2025, generation not stated)
Employment: Full-time professor, education; instructional design and oral communication
Household: 2 others (one adult, one child); one dependent; fish and chickens
Vision: Stargardt's macular degeneration since age 8, 48 years, progressive. Sees to about elbow distance, contrast-dependent, farsighted. Never learned braille.
Usage: Daily when a need arises, sometimes a week between uses
Tools they use: Meta glasses, closed-circuit television magnifier, Microsoft Universal Reader, Alexa, Gemini, ChatGPT, wired Sony headphones, Samsung Note 9
Notable: Referred by his eye doctor. Family vetoed face enrollment. Names public touchscreens, card readers and ticket machines as the single greatest barrier, ahead of anything the glasses do. Wants a tool, not a companion. Designs his curriculum so the visual task never has to happen.

Employment: Unemployed; training for a food licence and a vending business
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Seeing AI, Be My Eyes, Aira (free five minutes only), Soundscape, a standalone money counter, Alexa, a chatbot daily, Facebook owner groups
Notable: Has never tried Live AI and was unsure it exists. Learns about updates through Facebook groups rather than the vendor. Identifies eye drops with the glasses, then marks the bottle with a rubber band. Comfortable having his credit card and state ID number read aloud.

Persona: Blind creator and unpaid accessibility tester, AI-sceptical
Device: Ray-Ban Meta gen 1, plus a second identical pair
Employment: Unemployed; unpaid accessibility testing; runs a tech-review channel
Household: 4 others (parents, brother, grandfather); no dependents; pets
Vision: Born with retinopathy of prematurity, partial sight until 2023, then total loss following cataracts
Usage: Reduced from heavy to occasional. Battery degradation and face pressure named as the causes.
Tools they use: Meta glasses, Be My Eyes (primary), Be My AI, Seeing AI, ChatGPT, Gemini, Alexa, Envision Ally (tester), an AI email app (tester)
Notable: Used a volunteer looking through the glasses to play a mainstream shooter with no screen reader support. Also an Easter egg hunt and an iPad stuck in recovery mode. Rates Meta AI 2 of 5 and routes most visual work to a human instead. The sealed, non-replaceable battery is his top structural complaint.

Persona: Social navigator, venue-first user, continuous-narration adopter
Device: Ray-Ban Meta (bought August 2025, generation not stated)
Tools they use: Meta glasses, ScribeMe (continuous narration), Seeing AI, Lookout, Be My Eyes connected to the glasses, Aira, Gemini, Alexa Plus, screen reader
Notable: The study's first user of a third-party continuous narration app alongside the glasses, and the sharpest critic of it. Wants head-level hazard calls, a pause gesture and a content filter. Found the accessibility setting for detailed descriptions himself. Will not use it in a bathroom. Retired currency reading after seeing it fail in someone else's video.
